title: Find Factorial!
description:
Write a program to find the factorial of A using recursion. Factorial(N) = product of 1..N.

Problem Constraints
0 ≤ A ≤ 12

Example
A = 4 → 24. A = 1 → 1.
story: Base: 0! = 1. Recursive: N! = N × (N-1)!. Linear stack depth.
plain: Two parts: BASE CASE — if A == 0, return 1 (0! is 1 by convention). RECURSIVE CASE — return A * solve(A-1). Each frame multiplies its own A by the result of the smaller subproblem. Stack depth = A+1.
tale: A stack of boxes, each labelled with a number, gets unpacked from N down to 0. The bottom box contains '1'. As you re-pack, each box multiplies its own label into the running product.

solutions.label: Optimal — Linear Recursion
solutions.plain: Base case 0 → 1. Otherwise return A * solve(A-1).
solutions.tale: Unpack to zero, then re-multiply on the way back.
solutions.pseudocode: f(A) = 1 if A==0 else A * f(A-1)
solutions.story: Optimal for recursive form. Iterative loop saves stack.

data.footer: Factorial recursion for A=6 — unpack & repack the call stack.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: solve(6) called. Stack will grow to depth 7 (6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0).
script.overlay: Base case halts unbounded growth — without it, infinite recursion.

script.label: Repack: 1 → 1×1=1 → 2×1=2 → 3×2=6 → 4×6=24 → 5×24=120 → 6×120=720
script.msg: Each return multiplies the local A.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Overflow: for A ≥ 13, the result overflows int32. Constraint A ≤ 12 keeps us safe.

title: Find Fibonacci - II
description:
Fibonacci sequence: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … Fn = Fn-1 + Fn-2. Given A, return A-th Fibonacci using recursion. F0 = 0, F1 = 1.

Problem Constraints
0 ≤ A ≤ 20

Example
A = 2 → 1. A = 9 → 34.
story: Two base cases (0 → 0, 1 → 1). Recursive: f(A) = f(A-1) + f(A-2). Branching factor 2 → O(φ^N) calls.
plain: TWO base cases: A == 0 → 0, A == 1 → 1. Otherwise f(A) = f(A-1) + f(A-2). Naively exponential (~φ^N nodes in the call tree) because subtrees overlap massively — solve(A-2) is computed inside both branches. Memoisation reduces it to O(N).
tale: A genealogist asks each person 'who are your two predecessors?' until reaching the original ancestors (0 and 1). Each ancestor lookup is repeated many times — a wasteful family tree.

solutions.label: Brute — Tree Recursion
solutions.tale: Walk the whole genealogy every time.
solutions.pseudocode: f(A) = 0 if A==0; 1 if A==1; else f(A-1)+f(A-2)
solutions.story: Brute. Acceptable only for small A (constraint ≤ 20).

solutions.label: Optimal — Iterative Roll-Up
solutions.plain: Roll two variables forward — no recursion needed.
solutions.tale: Walk forward keeping just the last two terms.
approach: a = 0, b = 1. Loop i = 2..A: c = a + b; a = b; b = c. Return (A == 0 ? 0 : b).
solutions.pseudocode: a=0, b=1; loop i=2..A: c=a+b; a=b; b=c

data.footer: Fibonacci sequence to index 10. Iterative roll.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Recursive call tree for A=10 has ~177 nodes; iterative has 9 additions.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Lesson: recursion with overlapping subproblems → use memoisation (top-down DP) or iterate bottom-up.

title: Print 1 to A
description:
Given integer A, print numbers from 1 to A using recursion. Add a newline after.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A ≤ 10^4

Example
A = 5 → '1 2 3 4 5'.
story: Recurse FIRST with N-1, THEN print N. Stack unwinding prints in ascending order.
plain: Trick is the ORDER: recurse first, print after. The function dives all the way to base (N==0), then unwinds — and on each unwind frame, prints its N. So you get 1, 2, 3, …, A. If you printed BEFORE recursing, you'd get A down to 1.
tale: A diver descends N rungs of a ladder; on each climb back up, he calls out the current rung number — so he calls out 1, 2, …, N as he ascends.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Recurse on N-1 first, then print N. Print newline at the end.
solutions.tale: Print on the way back up.
solutions.pseudocode: f(N): if N==0 return; f(N-1); print N

data.footer: Print 1..A via recursion. Recurse first, print after.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Where you do work matters: before vs after recursive call inverts the order.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Print-before vs print-after: swap the two statements and you get '5 4 3 2 1'.

title: Print A to 1
description:
Given integer A, print numbers from A to 1 using recursion. Add a newline after.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A ≤ 10^4

Example
A = 5 → '5 4 3 2 1'.
story: Print FIRST, THEN recurse with N-1. Top of the stack prints first — descending.
plain: Swap the order from Print 1-to-A: print N FIRST, then recurse on N-1. Each frame prints before diving deeper, so the highest values print first.
tale: A diver standing at rung N shouts 'N!' before descending one rung. He shouts N, N-1, …, 1 on the way down.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Print N, then recurse on N-1.
solutions.pseudocode: f(N): if N==0 return; print N; f(N-1)

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Tail recursion friendly: work happens before the recursive call, so a compiler could optimise to a loop.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Compare with previous problem: same recursion, opposite work order → opposite print order.

title: Decreasing-Increasing in One Function
description:
Given positive N, print N, N-1, …, 1, 1, 2, …, N using a SINGLE recursive function. No loops.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 100

Example
N = 4 → '4 3 2 1 1 2 3 4'. N = 1 → '1 1'.
story: Each frame: print N → recurse(N-1) → print N. Stack mirror produces the palindrome-like output.
plain: Each frame prints N TWICE — once before recursing (descending sweep) and once after returning (ascending sweep). The recursion descends to the base, leaving the descending half printed; then unwinds, the second print happens on the way up.
tale: A bell-ringer walks down N stairs ringing once on each step. At the bottom he turns around and rings each step again on the way up. The result echoes from N → 1 → 1 → N.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Print N, recurse N-1, print N. Two prints per frame.
solutions.tale: Ring on the way down and the way up.
solutions.pseudocode: f(N): if N==0 return; print N; f(N-1); print N

data.footer: Decreasing-Increasing — N=5. Single function prints both halves.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Two prints per frame — descending leg before recurse, ascending leg after.

script.label: Descend: 5,4,3,2,1
script.msg: Each frame prints N then recurses → descending half emitted.

script.label: Ascend: 1,2,3,4,5
script.msg: Each frame returns from recurse, prints N → ascending half emitted.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Pattern: any palindromic output can be produced by putting symmetric work on both sides of the recursive call.

title: Check Palindrome
description:
Recursive function that returns 1 if A is a palindrome, else 0. Lowercase letters only.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ |A| ≤ 50000

Example
'naman' → 1. 'strings' → 0.
story: Two indices start, end. Base: start >= end → true. Else: A[start] == A[end] AND recurse(start+1, end-1).
plain: Use a helper f(start, end). Base: if start >= end (crossed or met), return true. Otherwise check A[start] == A[end] AND f(start+1, end-1). Stack depth N/2.
tale: Two readers stand at opposite ends of a scroll, reading inward. If their letters match at every step and they meet in the middle, the scroll is a palindrome.

solutions.label: Optimal
approach: Helper f(arr, start, end): if start >= end → return true; if arr[start] != arr[end] → return false; return f(arr, start+1, end-1).
solutions.pseudocode: f(s,e): if s>=e: true; if A[s]!=A[e]: false; return f(s+1,e-1)
solutions.story: Optimal. Iterative loop also works; constraint allows recursion.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Early exit: the first mismatch short-circuits — no need to walk the rest.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Iterative variant: a while loop with two pointers — same logic without the stack.

title: Tower of Hanoi
description:
Move A disks from tower 1 to tower 3 using tower 2 as helper. One disk at a time, never place a larger disk on a smaller one. Return the move sequence as a 2D array, each row [disk, from, to].

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A ≤ 18

Example
A = 2 → [[1,1,2],[2,1,3],[1,2,3]]. A = 3 → 7 moves.
story: Solve N: move N-1 from source→helper (using destination), move disk N from source→destination, move N-1 from helper→destination (using source). 2^N - 1 moves.
plain: Recursive reduction: to move N disks source→dest with helper, first move the top N-1 source→helper (using dest as temporary), then move disk N source→dest (1 move), then move N-1 helper→dest (using source as temporary). Minimum number of moves = 2^N - 1.
tale: An ancient monastery has three pegs and a tower of golden discs. The high priest delegates: 'apprentice, shift the top N-1 off the way; I'll move the big disc; then apprentice, finish.' The apprentices recursively delegate to smaller apprentices until they hold a single disc each.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: f(N, src, hlp, dst): if N==0 return; f(N-1, src, dst, hlp); record [N, src, dst]; f(N-1, hlp, src, dst).
approach: Helper hanoi(n, source, helper, destination, result).
Recurse hanoi(n-1, source, destination, helper, result) — shift smaller stack onto helper.
Recurse hanoi(n-1, helper, source, destination, result) — shift smaller stack onto destination.
solutions.pseudocode: hanoi(n, s, h, d): if n==0 return; hanoi(n-1, s, d, h); emit [n,s,d]; hanoi(n-1, h, s, d)
solutions.story: Optimal. Exponential output is unavoidable — that's the number of moves.

data.footer: Tower of Hanoi, A=3. Total moves = 2^3 − 1 = 7.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Tower 1 holds discs [3, 2, 1] (bottom→top). Goal: move to Tower 3.
script.overlay: Recurrence: T(N) = 2*T(N-1) + 1, T(1) = 1 → T(N) = 2^N − 1.

script.label: Move 5,6,7: disc 1 T2→T1, disc 2 T2→T3, disc 1 T1→T3
script.msg: Restack on T3 in 3 more moves.

script.label: DONE
script.msg: All 3 discs on Tower 3 in 7 moves. Move list captured.
script.overlay: Sequence of disc movements: the smallest disc moves every other turn — never the same disc twice in a row.

title: All Indices Of Array
description:
Given array A and target B, return sorted list of all indices where B occurs.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^3; B guaranteed to occur.

Example
A=[8,9,5,6,5,5], B=5 → [2,4,5].
story: Helper f(A, N, B): base N==0 → empty list. Else, build list for first N-1; if A[N-1]==B append N-1; return.
plain: Recursion that builds the answer list. f(A, N, B) returns indices in A[0..N-1]. Base N==0: empty list. Recursive: get the list for N-1; if A[N-1] == B, append N-1 to it; return. Because we process N-1 first and append after, the list naturally comes out in ascending order.
tale: A scribe scans a scroll from left to right; every time he sees the target glyph, he stamps its index at the end of his tally — so the tally is naturally sorted.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Recurse to build list for prefix, then append current if match.
approach: Helper f(A, N, B) → ArrayList: if N==0 return empty list.
Wrapper: call f(A, A.length, B), copy ArrayList → int[] in order.
solutions.pseudocode: f(N): if N==0: []; L = f(N-1); if A[N-1]==B: L.add(N-1); return L

data.footer: All indices where B=5 occurs in A. Recursion appends on unwind.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Order emerges naturally: appending on unwind = ascending index order.

script.label: Unwind: check each index
script.msg: Frame returns; check A[N-1]; append if match.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: If you tail-recurse with the list passed in as a parameter, no need to allocate at every frame.

title: Print Array using Recursion
description:
Given an array A, print elements left-to-right using recursion (no loops).

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ |A| ≤ 100

Example
A = [6,-2,5,3] → '6 -2 5 3'.
story: Helper f(A, N): base N==0 return; recurse N-1; print A[N-1].
plain: Same recursive pattern as 'Print 1 to A': recurse on N-1 FIRST, then print A[N-1]. Stack unwinding emits elements in original (left-to-right) order.
tale: A reader photocopies a stack of pages from top to bottom — but he can only see the bottom page. He recursively defers the upper pages to a helper, then once the helper is done, prints his bottom page last. Each helper does the same: defer up, print his page. The result is a clean top-to-bottom printout.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: f(A, N): if N==0 return; f(A, N-1); print A[N-1].
solutions.tale: Defer, print on the way back.
approach: Wrapper calls f(A, A.length) then newline.
f(A, N): if N==0 return; f(A, N-1); print A[N-1] with trailing space.
solutions.pseudocode: f(N): if N==0 return; f(N-1); print A[N-1]

data.footer: Print array recursively — A=[4,8,-1,7,2]. Recurse first, print after.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Stack grows N→0 with no output.
script.overlay: Compare to printing on the way down: that yields reversed order.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Alternative recurrence: pass an index from 0 upward, print FIRST then recurse — equivalent forward direction.

title: Fast Power (A^B)
description:
Compute A^B in O(log B) using fast exponentiation. Result fits in 64-bit long.

Problem Constraints
A^B fits 64-bit.

Example
A=2, B=10 → 1024. A=1, B=10^8 → 1.
story: Divide exponent in half. half = power(A, B/2). If B even: half*half. If B odd: half*half*A. O(log B).
plain: Halve the exponent at each step. half = power(A, B/2). If B is even: A^B = half * half. If odd: A^B = half * half * A. Base: B==1 → A. Reduces from O(B) multiplications to O(log B).
tale: Instead of multiplying A by itself B times, you square once and double the exponent. Like folding a paper — each fold doubles thickness, so log2(B) folds reach 2^B layers.

solutions.label: Brute — Linear Multiplication
solutions.plain: Multiply A by itself B times.
solutions.pseudocode: r=1; for i=1..B: r*=A; return r
solutions.story: Brute. TLE when B is large.

solutions.label: Optimal — Fast Power (Recursive Halving)
solutions.plain: Recurse on B/2. Square the half; multiply by A if B odd.
approach: If B is even, return halfPower * halfPower.
solutions.pseudocode: p(B) = A if B==1; h = p(B/2); return B even ? h*h : h*h*A

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Compute 3^13. Naive needs 13 multiplies; fast needs 4.
script.overlay: Recursion depth: log2(B) — for B=10^8 that's just ~27 calls.

script.label: Unwind B=13: 729*729*3 = 1594323
script.overlay: Modular variant: wrap each multiply in '% MOD' to handle very large bases without overflow.

title: First Index using Recursion
description:
Return first index where B occurs in A, or -1 if absent.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 100

Example
A=[-3,5,6,2], B=6 → 2. A=[0,1,0,2], B=3 → -1.
story: Walk index forward from 0. If A[i]==B return i. Else recurse with i+1. End of array → -1.
plain: Recurse from index 0 upward. Check current first; if match return index. Otherwise recurse on index+1. The first match wins because we check BEFORE recursing.
tale: A reader scans pages 0, 1, 2, … and immediately stops at the first match — never reads further.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Helper f(A, B, idx): if idx == N return -1; if A[idx]==B return idx; else f(A, B, idx+1).
approach: Helper f(A, B, idx) with idx starting at 0.
solutions.pseudocode: f(i): if i==N: -1; if A[i]==B: i; return f(i+1)

data.footer: First index of B=2 in A. Check-before-recurse.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Start at idx=0. Looking for first 2.
script.overlay: Short-circuit: first match returns through the stack without examining the rest.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Iterative alternative: a forward for-loop with early break — identical complexity, no stack.

title: Last Index using Recursion
description:
Return last index where B occurs in A, or -1.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 100

Example
A=[6,5,6,2], B=6 → 2. A=[0,1,0,2], B=3 → -1.
story: Recurse forward FIRST. If deeper call found a later index, return it. Else check current.
plain: Reverse the order from First Index: recurse FIRST, then check current. f(A, B, idx) returns -1 at end; otherwise gets the answer from idx+1 first. If that returned a valid index, return it (we've found something later). Else check if A[idx]==B and return idx or -1.
tale: A scanner walks all the way to the end, then back-tracks — at each step on the return, it checks whether anything later was found; if so, it propagates that index; otherwise it checks itself.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Recurse first, check after. Later matches win.
solutions.tale: Walk to the end, then walk back checking.
approach: Helper f(A, B, idx) starting idx=0.
Else if A[idx] == B return idx; else return -1.
solutions.pseudocode: f(i): if i==N: -1; r=f(i+1); if r!=-1: r; else A[i]==B ? i : -1
solutions.story: Optimal. Inverts the First Index order: do work AFTER recurse.

data.footer: Last index of B=2 in A. Recurse first, then check on unwind.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Order matters: recurse-then-check (this problem) finds the last match; check-then-recurse finds the first.

script.label: Unwind idx=5 A[5]=2 ✓
script.msg: rest = -1 so check current. Match! Return 5.

script.label: Unwind idx=3..0: each propagates 5
script.msg: All earlier frames see rest=5 and just return it.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Iterative alternative: reverse for-loop from N-1 to 0 with early return — same answer, no stack.
